title: The moths and the lamp
hookLine: insects flying into the oil lamps at night

lines: A PORCH LIGHT ON A SUMMER NIGHT.
cards: A porch light on a summer night. Moths come out of the dark, circle the bulb, bump it, drift off, circle again. A bulb is one thing.
An open flame is another: a moth that flies into a candle or an oil lamp doesn't come out again. Why do they keep coming? The Udana doesn't try to explain the moths.

teach.h: OIL LAMPS BURNING IN THE DARK.
teach.b: The whole story takes a few lines. The Buddha is sitting outdoors in the dark of the night, and oil lamps are burning.
Winged insects are flying around them and falling in, one after another, to their harm, to their ruin. The Buddha sees this, and, knowing the meaning of it, speaks a verse.
Rushing up, passing by what's essential, they bring on new bonds again and again, like insects falling into a lamp.

teach.h: BOUND BY THE SEEN AND THE HEARD.
teach.b: So some are bound up in what is seen and heard. That's all. No crowd, no question, no long teaching.
A man sitting in the dark, watching. Notice the phrase in the middle: passing by what's essential.
The moths aren't stupid. They're drawn by something real, the light. The trouble is that they mistake it for something it isn't, and keep coming back.
The verse says people can do the same with the seen and the heard: the bright thing on the screen, the voice that pulls at us, each rush tying another knot.
There's a link back to Bahiya, a few days ago: in the seen, only the seen. The moth doesn't stop at the seen. It flies straight in.
And the Buddha doesn't put out the lamps or explain the insects. He sits in the dark, sees them, and speaks about people.

how: Buddhist teachers sometimes use the image of insects and a flame for craving that harms the one who craves, drawing on scenes like this one in the Udana.

games.q: you're sitting outdoors at night and moths are falling into the oil lamps, one after another. what does the Buddha do in the Udana?
o: watch, and speak a verse about people bound to the seen and heard.
games.why: the text says only that he saw, and spoke the verse. the scene is short, and it's about us as much as the moths.

practice: Ask yourself what bright thing you keep circling, even when it burns a little: a feed, a fight, a craving, an evening that always ends the same way.
Picture it as a lamp in the dark, and watch yourself circling it with kindness, the way the Buddha watched the moths. You don't have to stop yet; just see the circling.

wordCard.voice: Adhipataka, a moth. In the Udana, insects falling into oil lamps at night: the picture of rushing again and again to the seen and the heard. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali adhipataka: a moth or winged insect. in Udana 6.9 they fall into the oil lamps.
